title: Return a Whole Dispatch
content:
What problem does this solve?
Dispatch work often needs a whole packet: destination, party, supplies, counts, and status. return can send a list or a dictionary — not only a number or string — so other code can keep using the result. A careful function builds a fresh structure instead of quietly changing the caller’s lists.

Previously in your program
You returned strings and numbers, and you built dictionaries in Lesson 13. Now you assemble a fresh dispatch packet and copy lists when the caller must keep the originals unchanged.

Basic syntax
  def pack_note(label):
      return [label]

  def route_summary(destination, stops):
      return {
          "destination": destination,
          "stops": list(stops),
          "stop_count": len(stops),
      }

What actually happens
If a function builds a list but never returns it, the caller receives None — the same None print returns. Returning a new list or dictionary hands ownership of that result to the caller. list(existing_list) is one clear way to make a shallow copy before you change anything; slicing or .copy() can also be correct. A dictionary whose values are lists previews nested data; this lesson only needs you to store and copy those lists, not traverse nested structures in general.

When this is useful
Return a structured value when later code must keep working with the result. Copy inputs when the caller still needs the originals unchanged.
concepts: return can send a list or dictionary, not only a number or string
print still returns None; building without returning also yields None
A function can assemble a fresh result instead of changing caller-owned input
list(existing_list) (or another clear copy) keeps the original list intact

examples.title: Built but forgotten
examples.explanation: The list is created, but nothing is returned, so print shows None.

examples.title: Fresh list for the caller
examples.code:
def with_flag(tags, flag):
    updated = list(tags)
    updated.append(flag)
    return updated

original = ["clear"]
print(with_flag(original, "reviewed"))
print(original)
examples.explanation: The returned list includes the new flag. original stays ["clear"].

common_mistakes: Building a list or dictionary and forgetting to return it
Returning inside a loop after the first item only
Appending to the caller’s list when a fresh copy was required
Printing the packet instead of returning it

exercises.title: Built but not returned
hints: Without return, a function yields None.

exercises.title: Preserve the original
exercises.prompt: Another part of the program still needs the original supplies list unchanged. How should a helper add one more item?
choices: append directly to the original and return it
create a new list, append to the new list, and return it
print the new item without returning a list
exercises.success_message: Yes — a new list keeps the caller’s original supplies intact.
exercises.failure_message: If the original must stay unchanged, do not append to it. Build and return a fresh list.
hints: Mutating the original changes what other code still holds.
Printing alone does not give other code a list value.
Choose the option that creates a new list.

exercises.title: Return after the loop
exercises.prompt: label_supplies returns after the first item because return sits inside the loop. Move the return so every packed line is included.
hints: Dedent return lines so it runs after the for loop.

tests.message: Keep a for loop inside label_supplies.
label_supplies([]) should return an empty list.
A single item should produce one Packed line.
Return after labeling every supply item.

exercises.title: Add without changing the caller
exercises.prompt:
Write add_item(supplies, item) that:
1. Creates a new list containing the existing supplies
2. Appends item to the new list
3. Returns the new list
4. Leaves the argument list unchanged

Any clear copy strategy is fine (list(...), slicing, .copy(), or equivalent).
hints: Copy the incoming list before you append.
Append to the copy, not to supplies itself.

tests.message: add_item should return a longer list and leave the original supplies unchanged.
Adding to an empty list must still preserve the original empty list.
Repeated values are allowed; still do not mutate the caller list.

exercises.title: Expedition Dispatch System v1
exercises.prompt:
Write build_dispatch(destination, party, supplies, status="Review") that returns a fresh dictionary with exactly these keys:
- destination
- party
- supplies
- member_count
- supply_count
- status

Rules:
- party and supplies in the returned dictionary are fresh list copies
- member_count is len(party)
- supply_count is len(supplies)
- status defaults to "Review" and may be overridden
- do not print
- do not mutate either input list
exercises.success_message: Dispatch packet complete. The warning from Expedition 17 travels with the record.
hints: Copy party and supplies into new lists before storing them in the dictionary.
Set member_count and supply_count with len on the inputs.
Include status from the parameter (default Review) and return the dictionary.

tests.message: build_dispatch must return the full packet with default status Review and leave inputs unchanged.
Positional status Ready must override the default.
Empty party and one supply must produce counts 0 and 1 with status Denied.
Do not hardcode destinations, names, or counts.

tests.expression: (lambda p, s: (lambda d: d["party"] is not p and d["supplies"] is not s)(build_dispatch("X", p, s)))(["a"], ["b"])
list((lambda p, s: (build_dispatch("Y", p, s), p, s))(["Aria"], ["map"])[1:])
